title: FRM Credit Risk, Lesson 5: Netting and collateral - cutting counterparty exposure
subtitle: For the same derivatives book, exposure can differ several times over because of a single contractual clause
whyItMatters: Since the crisis, most of the effort to reduce counterparty risk has gone not into models but into contracts and collateral. Understanding this mechanism is understanding why two banks with the same notional positions can carry very different counterparty capital.
openingQuestion: With one counterparty you hold two contracts: one showing a gain of 100bn and one showing a loss of 80bn. What is your credit exposure?
openingOptions: 100bn without a netting agreement, 20bn with one
20bn in every case, because the two contracts offset each other
180bn, because the absolute values of both contracts must be added
0bn, because the portfolio as a whole still carries positive value
explanation: Without a netting agreement, when the counterparty fails the administrator will demand the full 80bn on the contract where you are out of the money, while the 100bn owed to you queues up alongside the other creditors. That is cherry-picking, and it makes the true exposure 100bn. A legally enforceable netting agreement turns the entire relationship into a single net obligation, pulling exposure down to 20bn. This is why the legal enforceability of the netting clause in each jurisdiction is the first question, ahead of any calculation.

diagram.label: Gross exposure: the sum of the contracts with positive value
Netting: combine positives and negatives into one net obligation
Collateral: deduct what has been received, after the haircut
What remains is what carries capital and drives CVA

realWorldExample.company: The ISDA master agreement and the credit support annex
realWorldExample.description: The master agreement standardises the relationship between two parties into a single contract, which is what makes netting effective when one of them fails. The credit support annex sets the threshold, the minimum transfer amount and the revaluation frequency - those three parameters determine the residual exposure more than any model applied afterwards.

quiz.question: What does cherry-picking mean in the context of a counterparty default?
options: The regulator picks which contracts are paid first in a wind-down
The surviving party keeps the contracts that have positive value
The two parties agree to tear up the contracts nearest maturity
The failed party claims the favourable contracts and drops the rest
quiz.explanation: The insolvency administrator has a duty to maximise value for creditors, so they demand payment in full on the contracts where the other side owes money and leave their own payables queuing with everyone else. Legally enforceable netting is the only thing that stops this. Note the direction: the choice belongs to the estate of the failed party, not to the survivor and certainly not to the supervisor, and it is exercised unilaterally rather than negotiated between the two parties.

quiz.question: What does the threshold in a credit support annex do?
options: Exposure below it does not yet trigger a collateral transfer
The maximum collateral that may be received from the counterparty
The discount applied to the value of collateral received
The maximum number of days allowed to deliver after a call
quiz.explanation: The threshold is the unsecured exposure the two parties agree to extend to each other, usually linked to credit rating. A higher threshold means less collateral moving back and forth but a larger residual exposure - a trade-off between operational cost and risk. The other three answers name genuine annex parameters that are simply not this one: the discount is the haircut, the delivery window is the settlement period, and the amount that must move once the threshold is breached is the minimum transfer amount.

quiz.question: Why does collateral received have to take a haircut?
options: Because the regulator charges a fee on posted collateral
Because prices can fall between default and liquidation
Because the receiver must pay interest to the party posting it
Because collateral is always valued above its market price
quiz.explanation: Between the moment the counterparty defaults and the moment the asset can be sold there is a delay, and prices can fall over that interval. The haircut is the buffer for that risk, which is why it is large for volatile or illiquid assets and small for government bonds. Interest is indeed paid on cash collateral, but that is compensation for the use of funds and has nothing to do with the size of the buffer, and no supervisory fee is levied on posted collateral at all.

quiz.question: Scenario: Net exposure after netting is 60bn, and 50bn of collateral has been received with a 10% haircut. What is the residual exposure?
options: 5bn (= 60 − 50 × 1.1, haircut added the wrong way)
10bn (= 60 − 50, ignoring the haircut entirely)
15bn (= 60 − 50 × 0.9, computed after the haircut)
60bn (= treating the collateral as not received at all)
quiz.explanation: Collateral is only recognised at its post-haircut value: 50 × 0.9 = 45bn, so the residual exposure is 60 − 45 = 15bn. Ignoring the haircut understates the remaining risk precisely in the cases where the collateral is of the poorest quality, and adding the haircut on rather than taking it off flatters the position further still.

quiz.question: Why does clearing through a central counterparty reduce systemic counterparty risk?
options: Because a CCP removes the need to hold counterparty capital at all
Because the CCP guarantees every loss without requiring any margin
Because trades cleared through a CCP create no collateral requirement at all
Because every party faces one counterparty instead of facing each other
quiz.explanation: A dense web of bilateral exposures is replaced by a hub-and-spoke structure, so one member failing does not propagate directly to the others. The trade is that risk concentrates in the CCP itself - which is why its margin requirements and default fund become a critical point for the whole system. Those requirements are the opposite of an exemption: cleared trades carry initial and variation margin, and members still hold capital against their CCP exposures.

practicePrompt.question: With one counterparty you hold four contracts worth +80, −50, +30 and −20bn. With NO netting agreement, what is the exposure when the counterparty fails?
options: 110bn (= 80 + 30, the positive contracts only)
40bn (= 80 − 50 + 30 − 20, on a net basis)
180bn (= the sum of the absolute values)
70bn (= 50 + 20, the negative contracts)
practicePrompt.explanation: Without netting, the insolvency administrator gets to pick contracts: they demand the 50 and the 20 in full on the contracts favourable to them, while the 80 and the 30 you are owed queue up with the unsecured creditors. That is cherry-picking, and it turns exposure from 40bn net into 110bn. The 70bn difference comes from no model at all - it comes from whether a contractual clause is present or absent. This is why most counterparty risk reduction lives in contracts and collateral; the model only measures what is left once those two have done their work.

keyTakeaways: Without netting, exposure equals the sum of the in-the-money contracts - because the failed party will cherry-pick
The threshold and the minimum transfer amount in the credit support annex determine the residual exposure
Collateral counts only after the haircut, the buffer for the delay between default and liquidation
A CCP replaces the bilateral web with a hub-and-spoke structure, trading contagion risk for concentration risk

summary.keyIdea: Most counterparty risk reduction lives in contractual terms and the collateral mechanism, not in the model. The model only measures what is left once those two have done their work.

application.message: When comparing two banks of the same derivatives size, find the disclosure on netting and collateral. The gap in net exposure between them is usually far larger than the gap in notional size.

sections.text: Two contracts with the same counterparty, one up 100 and one down 80. The question of how much exposure there is has no answer until you know what the master agreement says.

Intuition says two opposing amounts cancel out. In insolvency they do not: the administrator has a duty to collect as much as possible for creditors, so they demand the amount you owe in full and leave the amount owed to you queuing with everyone else. Only a netting agreement that is legally enforceable in that particular jurisdiction turns the whole relationship into a single net obligation.
Three parameters decide what is left

The threshold is the level of exposure that needs no collateral. The minimum transfer amount is the smallest amount worth moving, so that trivial sums are not shuttled back and forth. The revaluation frequency decides how much exposure can build up between two calls. These three numbers affect real risk more than most of the modelling choices made behind them.

Receiving corporate bonds as collateral is not the same as receiving money. Between the counterparty defaulting and the sale going through, prices can fall - and they usually fall hardest at exactly that moment, because the same shock caused both. The haircut is the buffer for that delay, which is why it has to be larger for volatile or hard-to-sell assets.

sections.label: Worth remembering
sections.text: The first question before any exposure calculation is not which model to use, but whether the netting clause is legally enforceable in the counterparty's jurisdiction.
